analysis.title: A week with APEC consequences?
key_insights: A third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East and Israeli representatives met US officials on new strikes. Trump reportedly told advisers he may not attack Iran absent new provocations, partly at the request of Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.

Escalation continues despite that: the Houthis claim strikes on an airport and financial centre in Riyadh, and Tehran launched a drone strike at a US base in Bahrain, which Iran calls a response to hostile US actions.

Iran's Ghalibaf says Tehran is still willing to discuss a peace deal if the US accepts Iran's 'logical conditions'. Iran will not remain in 'neither war nor peace', and Deputy Minister Gharibabadi says the White House is using diplomacy to buy time for another attack.
The Houthis have forced Yemen's forces to retreat and again control the Bab al-Mandeb strait. They say they are no threat to international shipping and will target only Saudi Arabian vessels.
Oil has risen off its recent lows on these tensions and on reports that up to five ships hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre has confirmed only one attack.

The APEC summit in Shenzhen starts today. Trump, Xi and Putin are to hold a trilateral meeting on the sidelines with no agreed agenda. Rabobank expects no immediate results, and China has so far avoided an active role in Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

A separate Trump-Xi meeting later this week will probably be dominated by defence and protectionism. A US-China military accident-prevention agreement is progressing slowly because of differing views within the US administration, and a US defence coordination centre with Japan, Australia and the Philippines both raises the need for it and complicates talks.

The US-China trade truce expires in January. The US accuses China of not meeting its side, rare earths are not flowing to the US at the desired pace, and the House China Select Committee report says China has undercut and monopolized various industries.

The affair between Nvidia's former CEO Huang and an alleged Chinese spy is speeding US efforts to tighten AI chip export controls. Democrats and Republicans are backing bills limiting overseas sales of advanced chips.

US allies have agreed to a joint list of key technologies and AI supply lines needing protection from China. The US reportedly plans to nominate tens of companies as 'national champions' for US AI adoption, a move Rabobank says will anger Beijing.

Treasury Secretary Bessent calls for a 'dramatic shake-up' at Nvidia while Huang eyes a comeback. Rabobank says the AI trade is trying to regain footing and the Anthropic IPO may be the next test of AI appetite.

Week ahead: US retail sales for October on Tuesday are the main event that day. Wednesday brings UK and Eurozone October inflation, US housing starts and the October FOMC minutes. Eurozone HICP is not expected to deviate much from the preliminary 4.0%.

Thursday has Eurozone labour costs, US jobless claims and the Philadelphia and Kansas City Fed surveys. Friday has Japanese CPI, UK and Canadian retail sales and EU and US consumer confidence, with markets likely to focus on Eurozone negotiated wages.

A heavy central bank speaker calendar runs all week, including FOMC Chair Warsh on a panel and fireside chat today, and Fed officials Barr, Williams, Waller, Musalem, Hammack, Kashkari, Goolsbee, Barkin, Paulson and Cook, plus many ECB officials including Lagarde.
